transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-12
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alice Morgan (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Product), Raj Patel (DataBridge - Head of ML), Maya Liu (DataBridge - Infra), Sofia Gonzalez (DataBridge - PM)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on INT8 vs FP8 quantization profiles, tradeoffs between quality and latency, and proposed next steps for a POC + benchmark on DataBridge's prompts. Agreed to share profiles + perf sheet, run an initial benchmark, and reconvene next week.

Topics:
- Intro / goals (customer constraints: latency < 200ms p99 for short prompts, cost targets)
- INT8 vs FP8: quality delta, latency improvements, hardware/kernel considerations
- Redwood Optimize recommendations and autosuggest profiles
- Benchmarks: test plan, dataset, rollout/canary approach, evaluation metrics
- Security/operational considerations for Dedicated vs Hosted serving

Action items (recap): see Action Items section in metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alice: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros then we'll jump in, ben will do the deep optimize piece, i'm alice from redwood, ben over to you.
[00:18] Ben: thanks alice, hey raj, maya, sofia, hi priya. today our focus is quantization profiles — we usually walk folks through INT8 and FP8 tradeoffs and then how Optimize suggests profiles based on your workloads.
[00:30] Raj: awesome, our main constraints are p99 latency targets under 200ms for the short chat completions, cost per 1k tokens is also a big factor, and we want minimal quality regressions for LLM summarization.
[00:45] Ben: understood. quick context: INT8 generally gives larger memory savings and can reduce latency/cost more aggressively, but depending on model and distribution you might see small quality delta; FP8 sits in between — closer to fp16 in quality with moderate perf wins, assuming kernel support.
[01:05] Maya: when you say kernel support, do you mean specific GPUs or runtime kernels? we run mixed A100s and H100s on prem.
[01:12] Ben: yeah both — some fp8 paths are better optimized on newer hw, there can be vendor-specific kernels; on H100 fp8 tends to show good speedups, on older A100s INT8 is often the more stable win. sometimes toolchains call it 'fp eight' or 'fp8' in configs — sorry autotran script sometimes writes it weird.
[01:35] Sofia: curious about accuracy — do you have numbers for rouge/bleu or embedding similarity drops?
[01:42] Ben: we usually run an eval harness: your eval set -> reference outputs -> quality delta. typical: INT8 can cause 0.5-3% drop on generative metrics for some models, FP8 often stays <1% on many backbones, but that's model and prompt-distribution dependent. we try to quantify with automatic metrics + human spot-checks.
[02:05] Raj: ok, sounds fine as long as we can see the exact tradeoff on our data.
[02:12] Ben: exactly. Optimize helps pick profiles: we look at your seq len distribution, batch sizes, p95/p99 latency targets, and then recommend a profile — e.g., int8-aggressive, int8-conservative, fp8-balanced. it also simulates expected throughput and cost.
[02:35] Raj: does optimize do prefix / KV cache recommendations? our usage is a lot of short interactive sessions where prefix caching could help.
[02:44] Ben: yes, we factor in KV cache hit rates; prefix caching and KV cache retention settings are first-class in Optimize. for interactive short sessions, small KV caches + aggressive batching actually improves overall throughput without hurting latency much. caveat: batching introduces tail latency.
[03:05] Maya: how big is the batching effect? we care about p99 more than avg.
[03:10] Ben: it's workload dependent — for example on a 4096-token model, batching can increase p50 throughput by 2.5x but can push p99 beyond your target if queueing isn't tuned. our autoscaler and routing policies can keep p99 in check by favoring latency nodes for high-priority traffic.
[03:34] Priya: i'll share a slide that shows quality vs latency curves — we also include cost per 1M tokens as a separate axis in the perf sheet.
[03:42] Alice: quick demo: open the Optimize console... (short screen noise)
[03:51] Ben: on the left is 'profiles', you can see recommended profiles per model. here's an example for a 7B open model — int8-conservative drops memory 40% and latency ~1.3x, fp8-balanced drops memory 25% with latency ~1.15x but smaller quality delta.
[04:15] Raj: what about fallback policies — if int8 introduces obvious hallucinations, can we automatically roll back?
[04:22] Ben: yes, we support canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks. you can configure quality gates (e.g., eval thresholds on your prompt set) and if the quality metric degrades beyond the gate, traffic is rolled back to the previous profile and alert sent.
[04:38] Sofia: nice, how do alerts integrate with our stack — we use slack and pagerduty.
[04:42] Ben: out-of-the-box slack/pagerduty webhooks, and you can hook into tracing for granular analysis.
[04:48] Maya: on the private/deploy side: if we host on-prem, how much of Optimize runs in our VPC vs Redwood control plane?
[04:57] Alice: good question — for Private deployments, the control plane is customer-controlled; Optimize can run with a local agent to keep perf telemetry in your VPC; sensitive artifacts never leave without consent. we'll share the architecture doc.
[05:12] Raj: will we need to recompile kernels for our fleet?
[05:16] Ben: sometimes we ship optimized kernels; in Private you have option to use Redwood-provided kernels or build with our toolchain. for certain fp8 paths there's a small kernel build step on older OS/drivers.
[05:27] Raj: that's doable but needs ops time.
[05:29] Alice: fair, we'll note that in the next steps.
[05:33] (short cross-talk)
[06:00] Ben: demo continued — here's the perf spreadsheet we usually attach (link: https://redwood.ai/optimize/quant-profiles-perf.xlsx). you can toggle your seq len distribution and it will estimate p50/p95/p99 and cost.
[06:20] Raj: can we plug in our actual prompt set for more accurate numbers?
[06:25] Ben: yep, you can upload a sample set; we also accept hashed/anonymized tokens for privacy.
[06:32] Maya: about metrics: do you compute embedding drift if we quantize for embedding models?
[06:36] Ben: yes we run embedding-sim tests and measure cosine similarity vs fp16 baseline; for some embedding models INT8 can be pronounced, FP8 usually safer. we'll show you the similarity curves.
[06:48] Sofia: are there model families that you avoid INT8 on?
[06:52] Ben: certain LLMs with sensitive normalization layers show more regression with naive INT8; in those cases we recommend mixed precision or targeted per-layer quant. Optimize can suggest per-layer config.
[07:05] Raj: interesting — per-layer sounds complex to manage.
[07:09] Ben: Optimize abstracts it — you pick a named profile and it applies the per-layer knobs under the hood.
[07:17] (silence, typing)
[07:40] Ben: quick note on cost: INT8 often reduces memory footprint enough to fit larger batch sizes on same hardware, which compounds savings. FP8 gives modest memory wins but is sometimes easier quality-wise.
[07:56] Raj: rough ballpark numbers?
[07:58] Ben: generally back-of-envelope: INT8 could reduce token-cost 1.8-2.5x on some workloads; FP8 more like 1.2-1.6x. again these are bucket numbers — we'll run your set and produce exacts.
[08:16] Maya: ok thanks. also curious about inference latency for small sequence (<64 tokens) completions — jitter matters.
[08:23] Ben: for short sequences, kernel launch overhead and NVidia scheduler behavior can dominate; here we recommend minimal batching, low-latency nodes, and prefix caching if appropriate. Optimize can simulate short-seq microbenchmarks.
[08:39] Sofia: what about caching TTL — if someone disconnects and reconnects, do we keep KV cache?
[08:45] Ben: that's policy-driven, you can set TTL per route and we persist KV cache in-memory per session; for private deploys you can configure durability.
[08:57] Raj: security question: does quantization affect encryption or KMS?
[09:02] Alice: no, quantization is model runtime behavior. encryption at rest and in-transit unaffected. KMS still handles keys for logs and storage. we'll send SOC2/KMS integration docs.
[09:12] (brief pause)
[09:30] Ben: demo — here's a sample quality vs latency curve for a 13B model on H100: fp16 baseline (blue), fp8 (green) slightly left of baseline with near-identical quality, int8 (orange) further left but slight dip on some qa metrics.
[09:50] Raj: can we see the raw eval numbers?
[09:54] Ben: yep — for this synthetic set, fp8 preserves 99.2% of rouge-L vs fp16, int8 97.5% — again synthetic. we'll run your dataset to produce the real numbers.
[10:12] Maya: what's the effort to run a POC?
[10:15] Alice: typical POC: we request 1k representative prompts + expected seq len distribution and traffic pattern, we spin up a benchmark cluster (hosted or private), run profiling across 3 profiles (int8-cons, fp8-balanced, fp16 baseline), and deliver a perf + quality report. usually 5-10 business days.
[10:37] Raj: timeline wise procurement needs approvals — but we'd like initial bench results before EoY if possible.
[10:44] Alice: we'll aim for that.
[10:47] Priya: note on eval: we recommend both automatic metrics + a 20-sample human review for hallucination modes that metrics miss.
[10:55] Sofia: good.
[11:00] (pause)
[11:20] Raj: any gotchas with multi-model routing or fallback to smaller models when capacity spikes?
[11:27] Ben: yes, we do smart routing — traffic can be routed to lower-cost models or to dedicated pools; fallback rules can be set per route (latency-first vs cost-first). for example, if Dedicated pool hits capacity we can route to hosted equivalent or a quantized variant.
[11:44] Maya: do we need to change prompts when quantized?
[11:48] Ben: rarely, but sometimes tokenization edge cases show up; we recommend spot-checking prompts in the eval. Optimize flags prompts that change behavior notably.
[11:58] Raj: will you share the perf spreadsheet pre-populated with our token distribution?
[12:02] Ben: yes once we get a sample set.
[12:06] Alice: i'll follow up with the spreadsheet and the quant profiles doc. link again: https://redwood.ai/optimize/quant-profiles.pdf (we'll attach perf xlsx).
[12:18] Sofia: last question on pricing — how does dedicated reserved capacity interact with quantization savings?
[12:25] Alice: reserved capacity pricing is mostly compute-commitment-based; quantization reduces the number of GPUs you need or increases throughput per GPU, so it compounds cost savings — we'll provide example scenarios in the perf sheet with cost estimates.
[12:40] Raj: great.
[12:42] (small laughter)
[13:00] Ben: wrapping up — next steps: we'll get the profiles and perf sheet, you provide sample prompts and we run the bench. propose follow-up 2025-12-19 to review.
[13:12] Alice: thanks everyone.
[13:15] Raj: thanks all.
[13:18] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labels may be auto-assigned, there are small transcription artifacts (e.g., 'K V cash' for KV cache). Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.ai/optimize/quant-profiles.pdf, https://redwood.ai/optimize/quant-profiles-perf.xlsx
